fixes.explanation: A census counts heads, and the text never says anyone gets counted here. Jehoshaphat proclaims a fast throughout Judah. Nobody is told to count anything, friend.

A festival would be a party, and the text never calls this one. Jehoshaphat was alarmed and set his face to seek the LORD, and he proclaimed a fast throughout Judah. Then the people gathered to seek the LORD. Save the party hats for later, friend.

The text says the people of Judah gathered to seek the LORD, and they came “…from all the cities of Judah to seek Him.” It's a whole kingdom, not one crowd from the capital. Jerusalem isn't the only city on that list, friend.
Jehoshaphat prays that God gave this land forever to the descendants of Abraham, His friend. He says it right there in front of the assembly. I think that's a smart way to start when you're scared.
Moses doesn't show up in this part of the prayer. Jehoshaphat names Abraham, God's friend, as the one whose descendants got the land forever. Abraham is the name the prayer uses.
David isn't the name in this prayer. Jehoshaphat says God gave the land forever to the descendants of Abraham, whom he calls God's friend. Abraham is the name the prayer uses, friend.

A new king never comes up in what the people said. They said they'd stand before the temple and cry out in distress, and that God would hear them and save them. They already have a king, and he's the one praying. Hear and save is what they said.

Jehoshaphat says it plainly: “See how they are repaying us by coming to drive us out of the possession that You gave us as an inheritance.” Peace is the opposite of what he's describing. He's asking God to see how they're repaying Judah.

As they set out, Jehoshaphat says, “Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld; believe in His prophets, and you will succeed.” He talks about belief, and swords don't come up. That's the whole instruction, friend.

Jehoshaphat appoints those who would sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. They go out before the army, singing, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever.” That's what's out front, friend.

The ark isn't mentioned anywhere in this march. Jehoshaphat consults with the people and appoints singers to go out before the army. They sing to the LORD and praise the splendor of His holiness. I think that's a bold way to lead a march, friend.

The text says, “The moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir…” The timing is right there in the verse. The praise begins, and the LORD acts, friend.
It goes the other way. Once they finished off the inhabitants of Seir, the Ammonites and Moabites “…helped to destroy one another.” There's no peace treaty in this verse.
The text says that when they finished off the inhabitants of Seir, the Ammonites and Moabites “…helped to destroy one another.” They turned on each other instead of making peace. It's a hard verse.

Seven isn't the number here. The text says they were gathering the plunder for three days because there was so much. They found more than they could carry away. Three days is the number to remember, friend.

The text says, “…the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.” Every kingdom of the lands hears what the LORD did. The news reaches them, and the fear of God comes upon them.

Anger isn't the word here. The text says the fear of God came upon all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel. The kingdoms heard what the LORD had done, and that's when it came upon them.

The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, “…for his God had given him rest on every side.” That comes right after the fear of God fell on the kingdoms. The rest came from his God, and it covered every side.
No famine here. The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side. That's the opposite of trouble. Rest, not hunger, is the word the verse uses.
Tribute isn't mentioned in this verse. The text says Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, for his God had given him rest on every side. Peace and rest are the words the verse gives, friend.
